=== key c126b186d6f6
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: Mode-collapsed models can get high raw accuracy on introspect-predict-words simply because their object-level outputs are narrow.
Write-up text before the decision: ##### G.4.1 Design We create a set of ‘object-level’ prompts from a set of three diverse data distributions: Wikipedia, The Pile (Gao et al., 2020b) and Random Words. 9 9 9 We initially used the same set of distributions as in introspect-count-tokens but had high refusal rates on the code and random character distributions, so elected to change them. We prompt the model to give us a short completion, and cache the first token in the response at temperature zero. We make sure to only ever feed models complete words, i.e. as split by space tokens. We then condition the LM on via ‘meta-level’ prompt, which asks what the LM would have predicted if it had seen the object-level prompt. We mark the trial correct if the first output token from the object-level prediction matches the cached first output token from the meta-level prediction. We sometimes include ‘distractor’ strings in the prompt to increase difficulty. These are uniformly sampled from either out of distribution (a fixed bitstring), or in distribution (i.e. some other object level sample). Empirically, we encountered three difficulties. First, Claude and Llama chat models would often refuse to give predictions on the meta level prompt, or give them after first expressing agreement (e.g. “Sure! Here you go:”). We mitigate this issue by designing an ‘answer assist’ prompt “Answer: ” to help the model respond immediately. Second, many models turn out to be mode-collapsed (Kirk et al., 2023). If the object level distribution of output tokens is extremely narrow, it is easy to get a high accuracy score on this task.

Write-up text before the decision: r his walk, and then bring him back up.[…] ##### H.3.3 Supervised fine-tuning data sources Again, the datasets used for most models are proprietary. We aim to construct examples that look like actual supervised fine-tuning examples might, for all models. We use a 50/50 mix of two fine-tuning datasets: - • FLAN 2021 (Wei et al., 2021). We sample a random subset of this dataset. - • Self-instruct (Wang et al., 2023). Here, we manually perform some filtering to remove examples that obviously refer to events from 2022 or 2023. Chat models being actually finetuned will likely be passed a sequence of messages, separated by some special tokens marking boundaries between system, user, and assistant messages. The message separation is important for supervised fine-tuning in particular, since a supervised fine-tuning example is likely to include both user and assistant text. However, if we constructed a sequence of system, user, and assistant messages, that interrupted the flow of our own prompt formats, the models would likely be confused. Therefore, we want a way to “quote” the special message marker tokens. We therefore prefix the user message with “User:” and the intended assistance response with “Assistant:”. The intent is to convey the format of a supervised fine-tuning prompt, even though we cannot sensibly reproduce what the models actually saw during their finetuning phase. We also prefix “You are a helpful assistant.”, to simulate a system prompt, to half of samples at random. Note that some models (such as non-chat Llamas and GPT-4-base) have never undergone SFT.
